feedback: If a learner says 'the rock eroded' for breaking in place, separate the steps: 'Did the pieces move away, or just break? Breaking where it sits is weathering.'
If a learner treats moved material as having 'disappeared', ask 'where did the washed-off bits go?' and name the settling stage as deposition.

If a learner sees no obvious rounding and concludes nothing happened, point to the fines and clouded water — abrasion is real but slow, so the worn-off sediment is the measurable evidence; and remember sugar cubes only model rock and break, round and dissolve much faster.
activities.intendedInsight: Weathering (broken where it sits) and erosion (carried away) are distinct processes; freeze-thaw and abrasion both weather rock, and once material moves it is eventually deposited somewhere else.
learnerActions: Shake rock chips or gravel in a jar (with some water in it if you want to see clouding) and look for the signs of abrasion — fine sediment produced, water clouding if water is present, and edges gradually dulling. Visible rounding is slow, so the fine material worn off is the clearest short-term evidence that abrasion (weathering) is happening. Sugar cubes can stand in to show the idea quickly, but they dissolve in water and break far faster than rock, so use them only to illustrate the process, not to judge real rounding or rates.
Add water, swirl, then pour the water off into another container and watch where the broken bits settle — material carried away in the water and dropped elsewhere is erosion followed by deposition.

Run a freeze-thaw demonstration: soak a porous block or fill a crack in it with water (keep it wet between cycles), then repeatedly freeze and thaw it — as the water freezes it turns to ice and expands, pushing on the crack walls. Over many cycles this can widen the crack, flake off bits or eventually split the block, though a few classroom cycles may show only small changes; nothing is carried away (weathering in place).
For each observation, state out loud whether it shows weathering or erosion and what the evidence is.
Record how rounded/dulled the particles became and roughly how much sediment/fines were produced.
activities.title: Shake-jar abrasion + freeze-thaw: separating break-down from transport

feedback: If a learner says 'nothing happened' to the year-apart bank, use the photos to measure the small change: slow change still counts as erosion.
If a learner thinks only sudden events count, contrast a flood with gradual year-on-year wearing — both are erosion at different rates.
If a learner thinks harder rocks don't weather, note that all rock weathers, just at different rates.
activities.intendedInsight: Much erosion is slow and gradual, not only dramatic floods; measured change over time is still evidence, and features in real landscapes record the agents (water, ice, wind, vegetation) that acted on them.
learnerActions: Examine two photos of the same riverbank (or slope) taken about a year apart and describe what has changed.
Measure or estimate the small change (e.g. how far the bank edge retreated) and argue whether water could still be eroding it even though the change looks minor.
Classify features on a landscape image by the agent that shaped them (frost-cracked cliff, wind-carved rock, river-cut valley) and say whether each is mainly weathering or erosion.
Explain, using your measured stream-table results, why a bare slope often gullies and loses more soil while a planted bank usually holds better — and say whether your own numbers showed this.
activities.title: Reading real landscapes: evidence of change over time
